catalog_citation: Irshied, Omar & Michael Kenstowicz. 1984. Some phonological rules of Bani-Hassan Arabic: a Bedouin dialect. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 14(1): 109-147. Urbana: Dept. of Linguistics, University of Illinois. (archive.org scan studiesinlinguis131411983198…

catalog_quote: As in Levantine Arabic the major word stress in BHA is located on one of the last three syllables of the word--essentially the rightmost heavy syllable, otherwise the third last. Heavy syllables are those containing a long vowel (CVV) or a short vowel plus consonant (CVC), while light syllables contain a single short vowel CCV). At the stage of the derivation where stress is assigned extraheavy CWC and CVCC are only found in final position, where they naturally also take the major stress. A final CVC syllable counts as light in BHA, as ^n many other languages. If final consonants are ignored in the calculation of syllable weight for the assignment of accent then CVC will count as light while CWC and CVCC will still count as heavy. ... From these data it would appear that BHA has a version of the common Latin stress rule accenting the rightmost heavy syllable and otherwise the antepenult…
sweep_summary: The only title-keyword item, Taine-Cheikh 1988 (BSL 83), was already held by the project (HAL open scan, scanned) and was re-read: it is a syllable/foot/syncope study that marks stress in its transcription (circumflex on stressed long vowels, p. 226 n. 3; examples p. 229) but explicitly defers the stress-placement rules (pp. 249-250) and states no rule. The catalog's deciding source for hass1238, Irshied & Kenstowicz 1984, was downloaded from archive.org and describes Bani-Hassan Arabic, 'a Bedouin dialect of northern Jordan' (Zarqa-Mafraq-Jerash), not Hassaniyya of Mauritania; the mis-attachment comes from WALS code ahs (linked to ISO mey, plotted at 20N 10W) inherited by Glottolog as language code [hass1238]. The best first-hand Hassaniyya statement read is Taine-Cheikh 2007 (EALL II, HAL preprint p. 4): stress on the third mora from the end of the word (mäktäb vs mäktūb), a length accent salient only on long vowels; it should replace the Bani-Hassan quote as the deciding source. classification weight survives (moraic, quantity-sensitive) but the rule text should be corrected from 'rightmost heavy of last three, else antepenult' to 'third mora from the right edge'; the Bani-Hassan quote belongs on a Jordanian Bedouin / South Levantine Arabic record if one exists. Taine-Cheikh 1989/1994 open HAL papers and the 1988 Dictionnaire vol. 1 Introduction (HAL anti-bot block; low priority). for the session was exhausted, so relevance checks used HAL, archive.org, Glottolog and WALS records only.

new_statements.quote: Stress is on the third mora from the end of the word, e.g., on the first syllable in mäktäb 'desk', on the second in mäktūb 'written'. It is strongly marked only on long vowels (accent of length rather than intensity). A lot of grammatical morphemes are clitics.

new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive stress computed on moras: the syllable containing the third mora from the right edge is stressed — final syllable when it is superheavy (CVVC/CVCC: mäk'tūb, ktâb, debbûs), otherwise the penult (mäk-täb, zrî-be). Phonetically a length accent, salient only on long vowels; clitics join the host's accentual domain. This is a weight-sensitive system, so catalog classification weight stands, but the rule is moraic (third-mora-from-end), not the Levantine 'rightmost heavy of the last three syllables, else antepenult' in the current quote. Taine-Cheikh 1988's stress-marked examples (p. 229: ktâb, ezūzâl, debbûs, zrîbe, ṛaḥḥâle) are consistent with this rule.

sources.note: Explicit first-hand rule for Hassaniyya proper: stress on the syllable containing the third mora from the right edge (so final if the final syllable is superheavy CVVC/CVCC, otherwise penult when the final is CVC or CV); phonetically an accent of length, clearly perceptible only on long vowels. Quantity-sensitive, so compatible with the catalog's classification weight, but the rule is moraic and differs from the Levantine-type 'rightmost heavy of the last three syllables, else antepenult' rule in the catalog quote. sources.citation: Abdelhady, Saleem. 2025. Loan Words Stress System in Bedouin Jordanian Arabic: An Optimality Theoretic Account. Forum for Linguistic Studies 7(4): 14-22. doi:10.30564/fls.v7i4.8023
sources.tag: read: refines the catalog coding
sources.quote: Having in mind that BJA is quantity sensitive language; stress assignment goes through the following algorithm starting from the right edge of the word: Look for a super heavy syllable at the ultimate position: YES, assign stress => NO, look for a heavy syllable in the penultimate syllable; YES, assign stress => NO, look for a light syllable in the antepenultimate => YES, assign stress. Stop searching. [...] According to [10], main stress falls on the rightmost edge of the word. Moreover secondary stress is not allowed in that dialect.
sources.locator: pp. 21 (algorithm) and 16 (main stress rightmost, no secondary stress); foot type and extrametricality pp. 15-17; OT ranking pp. 18-21
sources.note: OT analysis of loanword stress in Bedouin Jordanian Arabic (34 words): trochaic feet left to right, quantity-sensitive, final-mora extrametricality, no degenerate feet; the Bedouin Jordanian variety covers Bani-Hassan.

sources.quote: In Bedouin JA, diminutives enjoy a variety of stress patterns. In patterns presented in (5a-f), stress falls on the initial syllable presenting a trochaic pattern. In (5g-h), the iambic pattern CCVV.'CVVC with its two distinct vocalizations C1C2ee.C3 +aat and C1C2ee.C3iiC4 takes place, with stress is assigned to the final CVVC (Watson, 2011; Mashaqba & Huneety, 2018).
sources.note: Reports that urban and Bedouin Jordanian Arabic differ in stress assignment on diminutives (urban iambic CVC.'CVVC, Bedouin a mix of trochaic and iambic patterns); the Bedouin Jordanian data bear directly on Bani-Hassan-type dialects.

sources.quote: L'accent de mot. Il n'est fortement marqué que s'il tombe sur une syllabe longue ou ultra-longue. Le plus souvent il affecte la dernière syllabe sauf s'il s'agit d'une syllabe brève — rappelons qu'en finale une voyelle longue est réalisée comme une courte —. D'un façon générale, l'unité accentuelle comporte le centre du syntagme et un certain nombre de clitiques (pronoms affixés, mais aussi les prépositions et la plupart des modalités nominales ou verbales : négation mā par exemple) : ktəb "il a écrit", kətbu "ils ont écrit", kətbû-he "ils l'ont écrite", kətbū-hâ-l-u "ils la leur ont écrite".
sources.locator: printed p. 178, section 1.1.3 'Structure syllabique et accentuation'; syllable typology p. 177; unstressed long vowels p. 176; tidinît p. 187-188
sources.note: weight-sensitive word accent: strongly marked only on a long (CVC/CVV) or ultra-long (CVCC/CVVC) syllable; usually the last syllable unless that syllable is short (CV; a word-final long vowel is realised short). Syllable typology p. 177: 'Les syllabes longues sont toujours fortes et les syllabes faibles sont toujours du type CV'; feet are S or W+S built right to left, and short vowels in open syllables marked weak are deleted, so the dialect has 'essentiellement des syllabes longues (CVC ou CVV) et des syllabes ultra-longues (CVCC ou CVVC)'. Domain: the accentual unit is the syntagm centre plu
